title: Twenty-eight flavors, one orange roof and two bad sales
lede: Howard Johnson’s did not go bankrupt. It was sold, split and converted, and what was left was licensed to its own franchisees, who ran out of restaurants one at a time.

chapters.title: A soda fountain, then a franchise
chapters.cap: restaurants by the end of 1939, mostly along highways on the eastern seaboard
chapters.body:
In 1925 Howard Deering Johnson borrowed $500 to buy a store in the Wollaston section of Quincy, Massachusetts, that sold candy, newspapers and patent medicines, and took on its debts with it. He revived the soda fountain with an ice cream that had almost twice the usual butterfat. By 1928 he was selling $240,000 of ice cream a year.[^1]

His first restaurant opened in Quincy in 1929. He had no capital to open more, so in 1935 he persuaded an acquaintance to build one in Orleans, on Cape Cod, and sell his food under his name. The licensee paid for the building; Johnson collected a fee and sold the supplies.[^1][^22] By the end of 1939 there were 107 Howard Johnson’s, with gross receipts of $10.5M.[^1]

image.caption: Howard Johnson’s in Nashua, New Hampshire, on a Tichnor Brothers linen postcard dated by the Boston Public Library to about 1930–1945. Public domain.[^27]
image.alt: Postcard of a white colonial-style restaurant with an orange roof, a cupola and a roadside sign

chapters.title: The turnpike contract and the war
chapters.cap: restaurants still open in the summer of 1944, down from about 200
chapters.body:
In 1940 the company won the contract for 24 restaurants on the new Pennsylvania Turnpike, and held that monopoly until 1979.[^1] The buildings were recognizable from a distance: orange porcelain roof tiles and a blue cupola, with the same 28 flavors of ice cream inside.[^1]

Then gasoline was rationed. In little more than a year the chain fell from about 200 restaurants to about 75, and by the summer of 1944 only 12 were open. The company survived by running cafeterias for war plants. After the war it built smaller units, and by 1954 there were about 400 restaurants in 32 states. That year it entered the motel business.[^1]

image.caption: The Midway plaza on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, on a postcard published by Howard Johnson’s own publishing department in Bedford, Pa., about 1940–1945. The turnpike restaurants were built of stone, without the orange roof. Public domain.[^27]
image.alt: Postcard of a stone colonial building with umbrellas on a terrace, captioned The Midway on America’s Super Highway

chapters.title: French chefs, a public company and 929 restaurants
chapters.cap: Howard Johnson’s restaurants at the 1961 public offering: 265 company-run, 340 licensed
chapters.body:
The founder handed the presidency to his son, Howard Brennan Johnson, in 1959. The son was 26.[^1] Around 1960 the company hired Pierre Franey and Jacques Pépin from Le Pavillon in New York to run its commissary cooking.[^13][^19] Pépin later recalled that in the mid-1960s McDonald’s, Burger King and Kentucky Fried Chicken together were smaller than Howard Johnson’s.[^19]

The company went public in 1961 with 605 restaurants and 88 franchised motor lodges. Under the son it bought back the profitable units: by 1963 company-owned restaurants outnumbered franchised ones. At the end of 1975 there were 929 Howard Johnson’s restaurants, 649 of them company-operated, and 536 motor lodges.[^1]

chapters.title: Stand pat, then sell
chapters.cap: paid by Imperial Group, announced September 1979, at $28 a share
chapters.body:
Highway locations produced 85% of the business, and the 1974 oil embargo hit them directly. Johnson stopped expanding. Customers complained of slow service and bland, frozen food. [Fast-food chains](/burger-chef/) and newer motel chains kept building.[^1]

In September 1979 Johnson accepted $630M from Imperial Group, a British tobacco, food and brewing conglomerate, for 1,040 restaurants and 520 motor lodges. Pretax earnings fell from $34M in 1979 to $14.7M in 1980.[^1] Franchisees later said Imperial spent $250,000 on restaurant services in four years.[^4] In September 1985 Imperial sold the company, without the Ground Round chain, to Marriott for $314M.[^2]

pull.text: I overreacted. I stopped all expansion, and once you stop, you know how hard it is to get the monster going again.
pull.who: Howard B. Johnson to Forbes, 1978, as quoted in the International Directory of Company Histories[^1]

chapters.title: The name goes one way, the kitchens another
chapters.cap: franchised restaurants passed to Prime Motor Inns in 1985, a hotel company that did not want them
chapters.body:
Marriott kept 350 company restaurants and 68 turnpike restaurants, and said many would become Big Boy outlets. It sold the trademark, the hotels and the 199 franchised restaurants to Prime Motor Inns for $235M.[^2] By the end of 1987 Marriott still owned 90 Howard Johnson’s restaurants, and by mid-1991 only 50.[^1]

The franchisees threatened to sue, and settled. On May 22, 1986 they incorporated Franchise Associates Inc., which received an exclusive license to the restaurant name.[^5] In 1991 there were about 110 franchised restaurants.[^1] By May 2005 there were eight, and the Associated Press could not get Franchise Associates to return its calls.[^6]

image.alt: Entrance of a Howard Johnson’s restaurant with an orange roof and a teal spire, photographed in 1999

chapters.title: Lake Placid, Bangor, Lake George
chapters.cap: Howard Johnson’s restaurant left in the country after September 6, 2016
chapters.body:
The Times Square restaurant, open since 1959, closed in 2005.[^23][^24] In 2007 the Waterbury, Connecticut restaurant left the system, which by then was run by a New York company called La Mancha Group. That left three.[^7]

Lake Placid, open since April 1956, closed at the end of March 2015.[^9] Bangor, open since 1966, served its last meal on September 6, 2016.[^10][^11] Lake George, built in 1953, had closed in 2011 and reopened under a former employee in January 2015.[^13] It shut for good in the spring of 2022, and the property was put up for lease.[^14][^15]
